listItems: Random weights break symmetry; their scale determines whether early signals survive.
Xavier/Glorot balances fan-in and fan-out and commonly fits tanh-like layers.
He/Kaiming uses a ReLU-aware fan-in scale.
Vanishing and exploding gradients arise from repeated chain-rule multiplication.
Normalization standardizes selected activations, then learns a scale γ and shift β.
BatchNorm depends on batch statistics during training; LayerNorm, InstanceNorm and GroupNorm use within-example groups.
Stable training is a system property involving data scale, activation, initialization, architecture, normalization, optimizer and learning rate.
captions: Conceptual illustration. Real activation distributions depend on the inputs, architecture, activation functions and the sampled weights.

Read left to right: if hidden neurons start with identical incoming weights, they remain copies under ordinary gradient updates. Randomness breaks that symmetry; variance scaling then keeps the random values from being too weak or too strong.

Real convolution tensors also contain height and width, and framework APIs specify exact axes. The coloured selection gives the core intuition: BatchNorm depends on other examples in the mini-batch; LayerNorm, InstanceNorm and GroupNorm calculate statistics within each example.
Calling torch.no_grad() does not switch BatchNorm to inference behaviour; call model.eval() as well.

codeBlocks.code:
import torch
from torch import nn

class SmallCNN(nn.Module):
    def __init__(self):
        super().__init__()
        self.features = nn.Sequential(
            nn.Conv2d(3, 32, kernel_size=3, padding=1, bias=False),
            nn.BatchNorm2d(32),
            nn.ReLU(),
            nn.Conv2d(32, 64, kernel_size=3, padding=1, bias=False),
            nn.BatchNorm2d(64),
            nn.ReLU(),
            nn.AdaptiveAvgPool2d(1),
        )
        self.classifier = nn.Linear(64, 10)

        # These convolutional layers are each followed by ReLU.
        for module in self.features.modules():
            if isinstance(module, nn.Conv2d):
                nn.init.kaiming_normal_(module.weight, mode="fan_in", nonlinearity="relu")

        # The classifier emits logits; no ReLU follows it.
        nn.init.xavier_uniform_(self.classifier.weight)
        nn.init.zeros_(self.classifier.bias)

    def forward(self, x):
        x = self.features(x)
        return self.classifier(x.flatten(1))

model = SmallCNN()

# Training: BatchNorm uses batch statistics and updates running values.
model.train()
train_logits = model(train_images)

# Validation/inference: use the saved running statistics.
model.eval()
with torch.no_grad():
    validation_logits = model(validation_images)

rows: ReLU or Leaky ReLU hidden layers
Accounts for the signal loss caused when ReLU sets negative values to zero.
Balances fan-in and fan-out to keep forward and backward variance useful.
Better scaled than arbitrary random values, but deep sigmoid networks can still saturate and vanish.
Use the activation, initializer and architecture conditions together; ordinary dropout breaks the intended behaviour.
Reinitializing the backbone destroys the learned representation; initialize only new layers unless intentionally training from scratch.

headings.text: Regularization: Teaching a Network to Succeed on New Data
The Real Goal Is Not to Win on the Training Set
Diagnose the Cause Before Adding a Remedy
L2 and L1 Add a Cost for Complicated Weights
One set of weights, two penalties
Dropout Prevents Dependence on One Fragile Path
A dropout pass with four activations
Early Stopping Uses Validation Performance to Choose Training Time
Label Smoothing Reduces Absolute Certainty in the Target
Distillation and Ensembles Solve Different Problems
Choose the Method That Matches the Symptom
A Small PyTorch Classifier With Three Regularizers
Common Failure Patterns and How to Investigate Them
What to Carry Into Your Next Model

paragraphs.text: Deep Learning · Generalization

A neural network can score perfectly on its practice examples and still fail in the real world. Regularization is the collection of choices that discourages this kind of memorization. In this lesson you will learn how to recognize overfitting, calculate L1 and L2 penalties, follow dropout with numbers, stop at the right checkpoint, soften labels, distil a teacher, and choose a method for a real project.

Imagine a student who memorizes the answers to one practice paper. The score on that paper is excellent, but a new exam with different questions exposes the problem: the student remembered examples instead of learning the underlying ideas. A high-capacity neural network can do the same thing with images, text or customer records.

Generalization means performing well on relevant examples that were not used to update the weights. Overfitting means the model has learned training-specific detail—possibly noise, backgrounds, duplicate records or accidental shortcuts—that does not transfer to those new examples. Regularization deliberately constrains or perturbs learning so useful, repeatable patterns have an advantage over brittle memorization.
Model A: impressive practice score
Training accuracy
Validation accuracy
The 21-point generalization gap is a warning. The training score alone hid the problem.
Model B: better real-world evidence
Although its training score is lower, the 3-point gap and stronger validation result make Model B the better candidate.
How a validation curve reveals overfitting
Lower loss is better. The values are illustrative, but the pattern is one you should learn to recognize.

A gap between training and validation performance suggests overfitting, but regularization is not the first answer to every gap. First confirm that the comparison is fair. Training and validation data must represent the same intended task, while remaining separate enough to prevent leakage.
1 · Verify the split
Keep users, patients, documents or time periods from leaking across splits. Near-duplicates can make validation falsely easy.
2 · Inspect the data
Check labels, class balance, preprocessing and whether validation contains a different camera, language, season or population.
3 · Compare both curves
High training and validation loss suggests underfitting or broken optimization—not a need for stronger regularization.

Regularization usually trades some training fit for better validation behaviour. If both sets are poor, adding more constraint can make the model worse. That situation may need better features, a more capable model, longer training or a repaired data pipeline.

Weights control how strongly one value influences the next layer. Very large weights can make a prediction depend sharply on small details. A penalty adds a second goal to the ordinary data loss: fit the labels, but avoid unnecessarily large weights.
L2 penalty
L1 penalty

Suppose the model calculated a data loss of 0.60 on the current batch. Its two illustrative learned weights currently equal 3 and 4. The developer chooses λ = 0.01 as a regularization hyperparameter; validation results—not backpropagation—decide whether that strength is suitable. We use the formulas exactly as written above; some texts include an extra ½, so always check the convention.
L2 calculation
L1 calculation

Interpretation: these totals are training objectives, not validation scores. The optimizer now receives pressure both to reduce prediction error and to reduce weight size. The numbers do not prove that L1 is "better" because 0.67 is smaller; the penalty shapes and useful λ values are different.

During each training forward pass, dropout randomly sets some activation values to zero. A neuron cannot assume that its usual partners will always be available, so the network is encouraged to distribute useful evidence across multiple paths. Dropout rate p is the probability of dropping an activation; keep probability q = 1 − p is the probability of retaining it.
Dropout changes the network only while it is learning
The crossed neurons are randomly inactive for one training pass. A different mask is sampled on a later pass.
Inverted dropout

Let h = [2, 4, 6, 8], an illustrative activation vector produced by the previous layer. The developer chooses dropout rate p = 0.25, so the calculated keep probability is q = 1 − 0.25 = 0.75. For this pass, the framework independently samples one keep/drop decision per activation and happens to produce m = [1, 0, 1, 1]. The mask is temporary; no neuron is deleted.
1. Apply mask m ⊙ h = [2, 0, 6, 8]
3. Interpret One activation vanished for this pass. The others grew by 1/0.75 so their long-run expected values remain unchanged.
One random pass does not need to have the same total or average as the original vector. The equality is an expectation over many possible masks.

An epoch is one pass through the training set. If training continues after the validation result has stopped improving, the network may become increasingly specialized to its training examples. Early stopping treats the number of training epochs as a choice to validate.
Early stopping keeps the best model, not the last model
Example: monitor validation loss, use patience = 2, and save whenever the loss reaches a new minimum.
Epoch 1
improved — save
Epoch 2
Epoch 3
Epoch 4
new best — save
Epoch 5
no improvement 1/2
Epoch 6
no improvement 2/2
Stop: after epoch 6
Restore: epoch 4 weights
Why: 0.39 was the lowest validation loss

Patience is how many checks we tolerate without sufficient improvement. A minimum change can prevent tiny numerical fluctuations from resetting patience. Most importantly, save the weights at each new best validation result and restore those weights when stopping. Keeping epoch 6 in the example would defeat the purpose.

In four-class classification, the ordinary one-hot target for a cat is [1, 0, 0, 0]. That says the correct class has probability one and every alternative has probability zero. Real labels may be imperfect, and forcing extreme confidence can make a classifier brittle. Label smoothing mixes the hard target with a uniform distribution.
Smoothed target

Where the values came from: four is fixed by the dataset's class list; [1, 0, 0, 0] comes from the known cat label; ε = 0.10 is a developer-chosen hyperparameter; 0.025 and 0.925 are calculated. Meaning: cat is still overwhelmingly correct, but the learning target no longer demands absolute certainty. Tune ε on validation data; smoothing can be harmful when confident, sharply separated probabilities are essential or when it removes useful information needed for distillation.

Knowledge distillation uses a strong, usually larger teacher model to train a smaller student . Logits are the raw scores before softmax. Dividing logits by a temperature T greater than one creates softer probabilities that expose relationships between incorrect classes, sometimes called "dark knowledge."
Knowledge distillation combines two kinds of supervision
Large teacher
cat 0.70 fox 0.22 dog 0.08
Soft probabilities reveal that this cat resembles a fox more than a dog.
Known label
cat 1.00 fox 0.00 dog 0.00
The hard label states the correct class.
Smaller student
learn truth + teacher pattern
The deployable model learns both the answer and the teacher's class relationships.
A common distillation objective

An ensemble , by contrast, keeps several trained models and combines their predictions. If three defect classifiers return 0.90, 0.60 and 0.75 probability of "defective," simple averaging gives (0.90 + 0.60 + 0.75) / 3 = 0.75 . Diversity is important: three nearly identical models often make the same mistakes. Ensembles can improve robustness, but serving three models costs more than serving one distilled student.

Regularization is a set of levers, not a checklist that should all be switched on. Begin with a reproducible baseline, inspect training and validation curves, then change one or two well-motivated settings at a time.

The model below uses dropout inside the network, AdamW weight decay in the optimizer, label smoothing in the loss, and a short early-stopping routine around the training process. Each line implements a mechanism already explained above.
Where the code's numbers and behaviours come from

In a production project, also save the optimizer state, epoch, metric definition and preprocessing configuration in the checkpoint. If biases or normalization parameters need different weight decay, create explicit parameter groups rather than applying one value blindly to everything.
Regularization cannot repair distribution shift.
If production images come from a new sensor or customers use a new language, the training distribution may not cover the task. Representative data, adaptation and monitoring are still required.
Validation can also be overfit.
Trying hundreds of choices against one validation set gradually adapts decisions to that set. Keep an untouched final test set and confirm important results across robust splits or repeated runs.

listItems: 64 inputs must match the feature vector supplied by the data pipeline; 4 outputs come from the four class names. The hidden width 32 is a model-capacity choice.
0.25 dropout, 0.10 smoothing, 3e−4 learning rate, 1e−2 decay, patience 2 and the 30-epoch ceiling are developer-chosen hyperparameters that should be validated.
model.train() enables dropout sampling; model.eval() disables it. no_grad() prevents validation from building a gradient graph.
Each mean batch loss is multiplied by that batch's size before division by the total number of examples. This sample-weighted mean remains correct when the final validation batch is smaller.
loss.backward() calculates parameter gradients, optimizer.step() applies AdamW's update, and state_dict() captures the best parameter values so the final model does not keep a worse later epoch.
Generalization—not minimum training loss—is the goal.
Use separate validation evidence to diagnose overfitting before adding regularization.
L2 discourages large weights smoothly; L1 encourages sparsity; AdamW applies decoupled weight decay.
Dropout randomly masks activations during training and is normally disabled for evaluation.
Early stopping must restore the best checkpoint, not keep the final epoch.
Label smoothing, distillation and ensembles all use softer information, but they solve different problems.
No regularizer replaces representative data, a trustworthy split and final testing.
captions: What to notice: the network continues to improve on examples it has seen, but after epoch 4 it becomes worse on separate validation examples. Regularization aims to improve that unseen-data behaviour, not merely to make training loss larger.
In libraries that use inverted dropout , scaling happens during training, so prediction needs no extra scaling. Calling model.eval() disables ordinary PyTorch dropout.
The teacher must already be trained (in standard offline distillation). The student is smaller, but matching a teacher does not guarantee equal accuracy.

import copy
import torch
from torch import nn

class Classifier(nn.Module):
    def __init__(self, input_features=64, classes=4):
        super().__init__()
        self.network = nn.Sequential(
            nn.Linear(input_features, 32),
            nn.ReLU(),
            nn.Dropout(p=0.25),  # random masking only in train mode
            nn.Linear(32, classes),  # raw class scores (logits)
        )

    def forward(self, x):
        return self.network(x)

model = Classifier()
loss_fn = nn.CrossEntropyLoss(label_smoothing=0.10)
optimizer = torch.optim.AdamW(
    model.parameters(), lr=3e-4, weight_decay=1e-2
)

best_loss = float("inf")
best_weights = None
checks_without_improvement = 0
patience = 2

for epoch in range(30):
    model.train()                  # enables dropout
    for inputs, labels in train_loader:
        optimizer.zero_grad()
        logits = model(inputs)
        loss = loss_fn(logits, labels)
        loss.backward()
        optimizer.step()

    model.eval()                   # disables ordinary dropout
    total_validation_loss = 0.0
    total_validation_examples = 0
    with torch.no_grad():
        for inputs, labels in validation_loader:
            logits = model(inputs)
            batch_size = labels.size(0)
            batch_loss = loss_fn(logits, labels)
            total_validation_loss += batch_loss.item() * batch_size
            total_validation_examples += batch_size

    validation_loss = total_validation_loss / total_validation_examples
    if validation_loss < best_loss - 1e-4:
        best_loss = validation_loss
        best_weights = copy.deepcopy(model.state_dict())
        checks_without_improvement = 0
    else:
        checks_without_improvement += 1
        if checks_without_improvement >= patience:
            break

model.load_state_dict(best_weights)  # keep the best, not the last

headings.text: Data Augmentation: Create Useful Variation Without Changing the Answer
Why One Stored Example Is Not One Possible Appearance
The Label-Preserving Rule Decides What Is Safe
Geometric and Appearance Changes Teach Different Invariances
Online Augmentation Samples a New View During Training
How many examples did the model really see?
Mixup Changes Both the Input and the Target
Build Separate Training and Validation Pipelines
Audit the Policy Before Trusting It

paragraphs.text: Deep Learning · Training Data

A model may see only one photograph of a diseased leaf during training, while the same leaf can appear brighter, shifted or slightly rotated in the field. Data augmentation presents realistic variations during training so the network learns what should stay the same. You will learn the label-preserving rule, choose safe transformations, follow Mixup numerically, handle boxes and masks correctly, and build separate training and validation pipelines.

Suppose a plant-disease app is trained only on centered leaves photographed in soft daylight. A farmer later photographs the same disease from the other side, closer to the camera and under stronger sunlight. The object and diagnosis are unchanged, but the pixel values are different. A model that memorized the training photographs can fail.

Data augmentation applies a sampled transformation to a training example before it reaches the model. The transformation might change position, orientation, colour, noise or even combine examples. Its purpose is to encode an invariance : a change the prediction should ignore. For this leaf task, a small shift should not change the diagnosis.
One training image can appear in several realistic forms
A plant-disease classifier should recognize the same symptoms when the camera angle or lighting changes slightly.

For supervised learning, each input x has a target y. A sampled transformation T produces a new input x'. If the transformation changes the meaning of the label, the target must change too—or the augmentation is invalid.
General augmentation rule
T ~ P(T) x' = T(x) y' = T target (y)

P(T) is the chosen distribution of possible transformations. For ordinary image classification, T target may leave the class unchanged. For object detection or segmentation, it must transform boxes, keypoints or masks to stay aligned.
Usually valid for a cat classifier
A modest crop or horizontal flip can leave "cat" correct if the cat remains visible and cats can realistically face either direction.
Potentially invalid for digit recognition
A 180° rotation can turn a handwritten 6 into something resembling 9. The transformation may change the class rather than preserve it.
Detection and segmentation targets must move with the image
A horizontal flip changes not only pixels, but also every spatial annotation.

Geometric transformations change where or how an object is arranged: crop, translate, rotate, scale, flip or warp. Appearance transformations change how values look without moving the object: brightness, contrast, colour, blur or noise. A good policy reflects the variation expected after deployment.

The magnitude matters. Rotating a street sign by 5° may model a tilted camera; rotating it by 90° may create an impossible road scene. Treat probability and strength as hyperparameters, inspect samples, and validate the whole policy.
Where augmentation belongs in the training pipeline
Stored sample
image + label
Random choice
flip? crop? colour?
Transformed pair
new pixels + valid label
Model update
forward → loss → backward

Online augmentation generates transformations as batches are loaded. It saves storage and can expose the model to different variants across epochs. Offline augmentation saves generated examples in advance, which can be useful when transformations are expensive or must be audited, but consumes storage and limits the variants to those precomputed.

Suppose the collected dataset contains 1,000 stored images; that count comes from the data. The developer chooses a 20-epoch training budget, and the loader samples one transformed view each time an image is fetched.
presentations = 1,000 images × 20 epochs = 20,000 training presentations

Interpretation: the network can encounter up to 20 sampled views per stored image. Do not report this as 20,000 independent real observations—the underlying subjects and information still come from the original 1,000.

Simple transformations keep one class label. Mixup instead forms a weighted combination of two training inputs and the same weighted combination of their label vectors. The mixing coefficient λ (lambda) lies between 0 and 1.
Mixup
x' = λx A + (1 − λ)x B y' = λy A + (1 − λ)y B
x A and x B are two inputs; y A and y B are their one-hot targets; λ controls how much of example A remains.
Mixup creates a weighted training example
x A
x B
blended input

For a transparent hand calculation, choose λ = 0.7. In real Mixup training, software usually samples λ from a Beta distribution whose shape is controlled by a developer-chosen hyperparameter. The cat and dog inputs come from the batch; their class IDs produce one-hot targets [1, 0, 0] and [0, 1, 0]. Because A contributes 0.7, B must contribute the remaining 1 − 0.7 = 0.3. Therefore the new target is 0.7[1,0,0] + 0.3[0,1,0] = [0.7, 0.3, 0] . The input pixels are blended with exactly the same two proportions, and the loss must accept soft targets. CutMix uses a patch from another image instead of blending every pixel, and weights the target according to the retained area. Both methods should be validated for the task; a visually strange mixture may not help specialized domains.

Random augmentation belongs in the training pipeline because it changes the learning problem. Validation should answer a stable question, so it normally uses deterministic resize/crop and the same normalization required by the model. Running random validation transformations makes metrics fluctuate and changes the examples being compared across experiments.
How to read the choices in this pipeline

Current torchvision v2 transforms can jointly handle images and supported targets such as bounding boxes and masks. Confirm that your dataset wraps those targets correctly and inspect a transformed batch before training.
View a contact sheet
Plot dozens of transformed input-target pairs. Human inspection catches cropped-away objects, corrupted text and misaligned masks.
Compare a baseline
Train with no augmentation, a mild policy and a stronger policy using the same split and seeds. Keep the simplest policy that reliably helps.
Track both curves
Augmentation often makes training accuracy lower while validation improves. If both collapse, the policy may be too strong.
Check class effects
A crop may remove small objects more often from one class. Report per-class metrics, not only an overall average.
Test deployment slices
Measure performance by camera, location, lighting, language or noise level. A global metric may hide a failure mode.
Make randomness reproducible
Record transform settings and seeds. For debugging, replay a failing sample with deterministic parameters.
Augmentation is a statement about the world: "If the input changes in this way, the correct answer should remain the same—or the target should change in this precisely matching way."

Next concept

listItems: 224 × 224 is the chosen model input size. The validation image is first resized to 256 , then centre-cropped to the same 224 × 224 shape so both pipelines feed equal tensor dimensions.

scale=(0.75, 1.0) asks the random crop to retain 75%–100% of an image-area range; p=0.5 gives each training image a 50% chance of flipping. The brightness and contrast limits 0.15 are mild starting hyperparameters, not learned values.

The three mean and standard-deviation values correspond to red, green and blue channels. These particular values are the conventional ImageNet statistics and are appropriate when matching ImageNet-pretrained weights; calculate statistics from the training split when using a different recipe.
Compose applies transforms in listed order. ToDtype(..., scale=True) converts pixel values to floating point and rescales ordinary 0–255 integers to 0–1 before normalization.
Choose transformations from real deployment variation and task semantics.
Apply randomness to training, while keeping validation repeatable.
Transform spatial targets together with their inputs.
Mixup and CutMix require corresponding soft or area-weighted targets.
Inspect examples and validate policies; more aggressive is not automatically better.
Augmentation complements representative data but does not replace it.
captions: The rule: each transformation should imitate variation the model may encounter while preserving the answer. A transformation is valid because of the task—not because a library offers it.
For a classification label such as "car," the class stays unchanged. For bounding boxes, masks or keypoints, the target geometry must receive the same random transformation as the image.

The original file can remain unchanged. The data loader samples a transformation when it fetches an example, so the model may see a different version in a later epoch. Validation and ordinary prediction use deterministic preprocessing instead.

The target must be mixed by the same coefficient as the input. The model is trained to change smoothly between examples rather than drawing an unnecessarily sharp boundary around every training point.

codeBlocks.code:
import torch
from torchvision.transforms import v2

# Random operations are sampled only for training examples.
train_transform = v2.Compose([
    v2.ToImage(),
    v2.RandomResizedCrop((224, 224), scale=(0.75, 1.0), antialias=True),
    v2.RandomHorizontalFlip(p=0.5),
    v2.ColorJitter(brightness=0.15, contrast=0.15),
    v2.ToDtype(torch.float32, scale=True),
    v2.Normalize(mean=[0.485, 0.456, 0.406],
                 std=[0.229, 0.224, 0.225]),
])

# Validation is repeatable: no random crop, flip or colour jitter.
validation_transform = v2.Compose([
    v2.ToImage(),
    v2.Resize(256, antialias=True),
    v2.CenterCrop((224, 224)),
    v2.ToDtype(torch.float32, scale=True),
    v2.Normalize(mean=[0.485, 0.456, 0.406],
                 std=[0.229, 0.224, 0.225]),
])

# The same stored file can return a new training view when fetched again.
train_dataset = LeafDataset(train_rows, transform=train_transform)
validation_dataset = LeafDataset(validation_rows, transform=validation_transform)

paragraphs.text: Deep Learning · Computer Vision

A Convolutional Neural Network (CNN) is a neural network built to learn visual patterns while keeping track of where those patterns occur. We will follow one image all the way from raw pixels to a class prediction, calculate a convolution by hand, see how filters are learned and reused, understand padding, stride and pooling, trace tensor shapes, and build a small image classifier.

Consider a camera above a factory conveyor belt. For each product, the system must answer: acceptable or damaged? A scratch may appear near the top, middle or bottom. It may be short or long, but its local visual pattern is similar wherever it appears.

A CNN solves this task in stages. First it learns small reusable pattern detectors. Early layers may respond to borders or colour changes. Later layers combine nearby responses into textures and parts, then combine parts into evidence for a whole object. A final classifier converts that evidence into scores for the possible answers.
What a CNN does from beginning to end
Values move from left to right to make a prediction. Learning later adjusts the filters and classifier weights.

The name now becomes less mysterious: neural network means connected layers with trainable weights; convolutional refers to the repeated local calculation used to create those early and intermediate feature maps.

A computer receives an image as numbers arranged in a grid. In a 224 × 224 colour image , the first 224 is the number of pixel columns across the image, the second 224 is the number of pixel rows from top to bottom, and the 3 is the number of colour values stored at every location.
224 pixel columns (width)
Zoom in on one colour pixel
The three aligned grids are called the Red, Green and Blue channels . They describe the colour at every pixel location.
Now compare two ways of connecting those 150,528 values to 64 outputs. A parameter is a trainable number—a weight or bias—that training is allowed to change.
Dense layer: every input connects to every neuron
150,528 inputs × 64 neurons because every one of the 64 neurons needs a separate weight for every image value.
150,528 × 64 = 9,633,792 weights + 64 biases (one per neuron) = 9,633,856 parameters
Convolution: 64 small filters are reused
3 filter rows × 3 filter columns × 3 RGB channels × 64 filters , plus one bias for each filter.
3 × 3 × 3 × 64 = 1,728 weights + 64 biases = 1,792 parameters

The dramatic reduction comes from two ideas. Local connectivity means one output examines a small nearby patch rather than the whole image. Weight sharing means the same filter weights are reused at the top, middle and bottom instead of learning a new copy at every location. The filter can therefore search for the same scratch pattern wherever it appears.

Before calculating anything, connect each term to a physical role. A filter is not a ready-made "cat detector." It begins with small weight values and is adjusted by training until its responses help reduce the loss.

Before calculating anything, we need to know what the filter is trying to do. A filter , also called a kernel , is a small grid of numerical weights. Instead of asking one enormous question about the entire image, it asks the same small local question at many positions.
3 columns
3 rows × 3 columns = 9 weights
The weights form a small pattern test
If a patch is bright on the left and dark on the right, the positive side contributes more than the negative side, so the total response becomes positive.

At one position, the layer pairs the filter with the equally sized image patch, multiplies values in matching cells, adds the products, and finally adds one bias. In our hand calculation the bias is 0 , so it does not change the result. The sum becomes one number because the purpose is to summarize how strongly that whole patch matches this filter.
One output at row i, column j
z i,j = b + Σ u Σ v X i+u,j+v K u,v
X is the input grid, K is the filter, u and v visit positions inside the filter, b is one learned bias for the output channel, and z is the filter response.
From nine matching pairs to one feature-map cell
Green marks the first input patch, amber marks the filter, and pink marks the output cell produced by their calculation.
5 × 5 input: first 3 × 3 patch highlighted
matching cells
3 × 3 filter
multiply, then add
3 × 3 feature map
Exactly what is multiplied
Each patch value is paired only with the filter weight in the same row and column. This produces nine products:

We add the nine products because together they measure how closely the whole patch matches the filter's pattern. The strong positive total, 3 , says this patch has the bright-left, dark-right change that our teaching filter rewards. One patch produces one summary number, so that number occupies one feature-map cell.
Move the same filter one cell at a time
Position 1
Rows 1–3, columns 1–3
result = 3
Move right → Position 2
Rows 1–3, columns 2–4
Visit all 9 positions
Repeat across each row, then move down
complete feature map

With stride 1 and no padding, the filter has three horizontal starting columns—1, 2 and 3—and three vertical starting rows. Therefore it visits 3 × 3 = 9 positions , producing the nine cells in the final 3 × 3 feature map.

The hand calculation used one 2D grid only to make the nine products visible. An RGB image has three aligned input grids, so a first-layer filter must look through all three. A 3 × 3 RGB filter therefore contains a 3 × 3 slice for Red, another for Green, and another for Blue.
An RGB filter covers all three colour channels
The earlier arithmetic used one grid so the multiplication was easy to see. A real first-layer filter for a colour image has depth as well as height and width.
3 × 3 × 3 = 27 weights
Add 27 products + one bias
one output value

A convolution is commonly followed by the ReLU activation function: ReLU(x) = max(0, x) . Positive responses remain, while negative responses become zero. For example, [3, −2, 5] becomes [3, 0, 5] . This lets the next layer focus on where the current filter produced a positive response. The Activation Functions lesson explains the function in full.

The values 1, 0, −1 belonged only to our teaching filter. A real CNN normally begins with small initialized filter weights. A forward pass uses them to make a prediction; the loss measures the error; backpropagation calculates how every weight contributed to that error; and the optimizer adjusts the weights. Repeating this cycle over many labelled images allows useful filters to emerge. The image does not directly supply the filter values, and the values do not remain fixed during training.
A CNN builds a hierarchy rather than recognizing an object in one jump
Every later value depends on a wider area of the original image, called its receptive field.
Pixels
light
dark

⌜ corner

curve

A receptive field grows through connected local views
Layer 1 value
sees 3 × 3 pixels
Layer 2 value
combines a 3 × 3 area of Layer 1
Deeper value
depends on a larger image area

Padding adds border cells around the input, usually zeros. It lets a filter visit locations near an image edge without hanging outside the available grid. Stride is simply how far the filter moves after each calculation. These choices determine how many legal filter positions—and therefore how many output cells—exist.
Padding changes what happens at the border
No padding
5 × 5 input 3 × 3 output
Padding = 1
zeros form a border 5 × 5 output

Without padding, the filter cannot be centred on an edge pixel without extending beyond the image. A one-cell zero border gives it legal positions around the edge and preserves the 5 × 5 spatial size when the filter is 3 × 3 and stride is 1.
Stride is the distance moved after each calculation
Stride = 1
Visit neighbouring starting positions.
Stride = 2
Skip one position each time, so fewer outputs are created.
The visual gives the intuition; the following formula counts the positions precisely. It applies to one spatial direction at a time, so calculate it once for height and once for width.
Output size for one spatial dimension
N out = floor((N + 2P − K) / S) + 1

N is the input height or width, K is the filter height or width, P is the border added on each side, and S is the movement step. floor means discard any incomplete final placement. This beginner formula assumes dilation 1, which is the default used in our code.
5 input cells − 3 filter cells leaves room for starting positions 1, 2 and 3.
"Same" spatial size
Padding 1 adds one cell to both sides, so 2P = 2 .
Stride 2
Move two cells per calculation instead of one, creating fewer positions.

After a feature has been detected, the exact pixel location may be less important than whether a strong response exists nearby. A pooling window is a small region examined at one time. Max pooling replaces that region with its largest value; average pooling replaces it with the mean. Neither operation has trainable weights.
4 × 4 feature map
2 × 2 max pool stride 2
2 × 2 result

Pooling reduces memory and lets later values summarize wider regions, but it throws information away. For tasks that need precise locations—such as segmentation—architectures preserve or later restore spatial detail. Many modern classifiers use strided convolutions for intermediate downsampling and global average pooling near the end. "Global" means the window covers an entire feature map: a 32 × 32 map has 1,024 values, and averaging them produces one summary value for that channel.

A tensor is a multidimensional arrangement of numbers, and its shape states how many values exist along each dimension. PyTorch image batches use N × C × H × W : number of images, channels, height in rows, and width in columns.
Decode 32 × 3 × 64 × 64 instead of memorizing it
N
images in this batch
C
RGB channels per image
H
pixel rows (height)
W
pixel columns (width)
Now follow those meanings through the complete model. Height and width describe where responses occur; channels describe which learned filters produced them.

The final linear layer produces one number per possible class. These raw numbers are called logits . A logit is evidence, not yet a probability: it may be negative, and the logits do not need to add to 1. Softmax converts the set into probabilities while preserving their order, and the largest probability becomes the predicted class.
Logits: raw scores
They may be negative and do not have to add to 1.
Softmax
Probabilities
They are between 0 and 1 and add to 1.
highest
Cat

The code follows the preceding table. In Conv2d(3, 16, kernel_size=3, padding=1) , 3 means three incoming RGB channels, 16 means sixteen learned filters and output maps, kernel_size=3 means each filter is 3 × 3 spatially, and padding=1 adds one border cell on every side.

For a real project, load normalized training/validation data, use an optimizer, call zero_grad() before each backward pass, and monitor held-out metrics. The previous training-loop and augmentation lessons cover those pieces.
Shape mismatch in the classifier
Print N×C×H×W after each stage. Prefer adaptive/global pooling when input sizes may vary.
Wrong channel order
PyTorch layers expect N×C×H×W, while many image arrays arrive as N×H×W×C. Permute deliberately.
Softmax before CrossEntropyLoss
Pass logits directly. Applying softmax first changes the intended numerically stable calculation.
Feature maps become 0×0
Too many valid convolutions or pooling operations shrink small inputs. Recalculate the output-size formula.
High accuracy from backgrounds
Inspect errors and saliency cautiously; collect diverse backgrounds and use valid augmentation.
Assuming complete shift/rotation invariance
Test controlled transformations. Use appropriate augmentation or architecture changes when the task requires them.

A CNN learns small filters, reuses each filter across an image, records the responses in feature maps, combines local responses into increasingly large patterns, reduces spatial size when useful, and turns the final representation into class scores. Backpropagation and an optimizer learn every filter from labelled examples.

listItems: Local connectivity asks about nearby pixels.
Weight sharing detects the same pattern at different positions with the same parameters.
Padding, stride and pooling control spatial size and information loss.
Channels hold different learned pattern responses.
The output-size and parameter-count calculations let you verify an architecture before training.
captions: This is a common teaching architecture, not a rule that every modern CNN follows. Many networks replace flattening with global average pooling, change the downsampling strategy, or use residual blocks.
224 pixels wide × 224 pixels high × 3 colour values per pixel = 150,528 numerical input values. We multiply by 3 because every colour pixel stores three numbers, not one.

Where did 1, 0 and −1 come from? We deliberately chose them for this hand-worked teaching example. They are not taken from the image, they are not universal CNN constants, and real CNN filters are not fixed to these values. A real filter starts with initialized weights and training changes them.

The complete feature map above has been checked against the shown input and filter. Deep-learning libraries commonly perform this operation as cross-correlation while using the familiar name "convolution"; they do not flip the filter first.
The labels above are conceptual. A trained feature map is a grid of numerical responses, and individual channels do not always correspond to one clean human concept.

The deeper value does not receive the whole original image directly. It receives earlier values that have already collected information from overlapping local regions. For two stride-1, 3 × 3 convolutions, a Layer 2 value is influenced by a 5 × 5 region of the original image.

The highlighted 2 × 2 window contains 1, 7, 5 and 4, so max pooling keeps 7 as the highlighted output. Stride 2 then moves to the next non-overlapping window. The four windows produce 7, 6, 8 and 9. Pooling lowers width and height, but it discards exact location and the other values; it does not change the number of channels.

During training, pass the logits directly to PyTorch's CrossEntropyLoss . It performs the softmax-and-log calculation internally in a numerically stable way. Apply softmax yourself only when you need readable probabilities for interpretation or display.

codeBlocks.code:
import torch
from torch import nn

class SmallCNN(nn.Module):
    def __init__(self, classes=4):
        super().__init__()
        self.features = nn.Sequential(
            nn.Conv2d(3, 16, kernel_size=3, padding=1),
            nn.ReLU(),
            nn.MaxPool2d(kernel_size=2, stride=2),
            nn.Conv2d(16, 32, kernel_size=3, padding=1),
            nn.ReLU(),
            nn.AdaptiveAvgPool2d((1, 1)),
        )
        self.classifier = nn.Linear(32, classes)

    def forward(self, images):
        maps = self.features(images)       # [N, 32, 1, 1]
        features = maps.flatten(start_dim=1)  # [N, 32]
        return self.classifier(features)   # [N, 4] logits

model = SmallCNN(classes=4)
images = torch.randn(32, 3, 64, 64)
labels = torch.randint(0, 4, (32,))

logits = model(images)
loss = nn.CrossEntropyLoss()(logits, labels)
loss.backward()  # gradients now exist for filters and classifier weights

print(logits.shape)  # torch.Size([32, 4])
print(float(loss))

paragraphs.text: Deep Learning · Architecture Design

CNN architecture names are useful only when you understand the problem each design tried to solve. This lesson follows the move from small digit recognizers to GPU-scale networks, repeated small filters, multi-scale branches and residual shortcuts. You will calculate why stacked 3 × 3 filters work, trace a residual block with numbers, and learn when a pretrained architecture is a sensible starting point.

The previous lesson explained convolution, feature maps and pooling. An architecture specifies how many of those operations are used, how they connect, when spatial size shrinks, how channel count grows and how the final prediction is produced. Changing the plan changes accuracy, memory, speed and how easily gradients reach early layers.

The classic architectures below are milestones because each demonstrated a reusable idea. Later models did not simply "add more layers"; they found better ways to use depth, computation and information flow.
CNN progress was a sequence of solved bottlenecks
Read this as a map of design ideas, not a leaderboard for today.

LeNet-5 was designed for small grayscale character images. Its recognizable flow—convolution, subsampling, another convolution, then fully connected classification—showed that a network could learn local stroke patterns and combine them into digit evidence. It is small enough to study, but its original activations and training context belong to an earlier era.
Read an architecture as a sequence of explained shape changes
The historical LeNet-5 flow is useful because every dimension can be followed. Shapes below use channels × height × width for one image.

AlexNet tackled ImageNet: roughly 1.2 million training images across 1,000 classes in the original competition setup. Its five convolutional and three fully connected learned layers were far larger than LeNet. GPU training made the computation feasible; ReLU activations trained faster than saturating tanh units in that setting; overlapping max pooling, data augmentation and dropout were important parts of the system.
Compute
The original network split work across two GPUs because the model did not fit conveniently on one GPU of that era.
Optimization
ReLU produced positive linear responses instead of saturating both sides like sigmoid/tanh.
Generalization
Random crops/reflections and dropout reduced overfitting in a high-capacity model.

VGG replaced a mixture of large filter sizes with a regular pattern: repeat 3 × 3 convolutions, then downsample. Stacking small filters gradually grows the receptive field while placing nonlinear activations between calculations. VGG-16 is conceptually clean and remains useful for education and feature-based perceptual losses, but its dense classifier makes the standard model very large.
Why VGG repeated 3 × 3 convolutions
Two stride-1, unpadded 3 × 3 layers give the second layer a 5 × 5 receptive field, with a nonlinearity between them.
first local view
second local view
effective receptive field
One 5×5 filter: 25 spatial weights per input-output channel pair.
Two 3×3 filters: 18 spatial weights in this simplified single-channel comparison, plus an extra learned nonlinearity.

A small filter is good for fine detail; a larger filter sees a wider region. An Inception module sends the same input through several branches and concatenates their output channels. A 1 × 1 convolution is more than a spatial filter: at each position it learns a weighted combination across input channels and can reduce the number of channels before a costly 3 × 3 or 5 × 5 operation.
An Inception module asks several size questions in parallel
Why place a 1 × 1 convolution before an expensive 5 × 5 branch?
Suppose one location has 192 incoming channels and the branch should produce 32 output channels. These channel counts are architecture choices. Ignore biases so the comparison stays focused.
Direct 5 × 5 convolution
5 × 5 spatial weights × 192 input channels × 32 output filters = 153,600 weights
Reduce to 16 channels, then use 5 × 5

GoogLeNet also used global average pooling near the end, avoiding the enormous dense head seen in VGG. The trade-off is a more complicated branching design. Modern descendants changed the exact factorization and normalization choices, but the multi-scale and bottleneck ideas remained influential.

Depth lets a network compose more stages of representation, but a deeper plain network can be harder to optimize. The ResNet authors highlighted a degradation problem : adding layers could produce higher training error, even when overfitting was not the explanation. In principle, extra layers could copy their input and do no harm; in practice, learning that identity through many nonlinear layers was difficult.

A residual block makes the easy path explicit. The main branch learns F(x), a change to the input, while the shortcut carries x directly. Their sum lets a block preserve information when a large change is unnecessary and gives gradient information a direct route backward.
A residual block learns a useful change while preserving a direct route

For a transparent teaching example, we manually choose the incoming feature vector x = [2, −1] and suppose the convolutional branch has calculated F(x) = [0.5, 0.8]. In a trained network, x comes from the previous layer and F(x) is produced by learned convolution and normalization parameters.
1. Main branch result F(x) = [0.5, 0.8]
2. Add matching positions [0.5+2, 0.8+(−1)] = [2.5, −0.2]

Why addition? It preserves the original signal while letting the branch propose a correction at each matching position. The gradient of the addition also contains a direct identity route back to x. Addition requires equal shapes; when shapes differ, the shortcut must first project x to the required size.

Parameter totals depend on the exact variant and classifier. For reference, Keras lists approximately 138.4M parameters for its standard VGG16 and 25.6M for ResNet50; depth and parameter count are not the same measurement.

This teaching block keeps the same number of channels and the same height and width, so the identity tensor can be added directly. Batch normalization and ReLU are shown in a common basic-block arrangement.
If a block changes shape—for example 32 to 64 channels with stride 2—the shortcut also needs a projection that produces the same shape. Tensor addition cannot combine mismatched dimensions.
Where the code dimensions come from: 8 is a chosen teaching batch size; 32 is the chosen channel count for the block; 28 × 28 is a sample spatial size. None of these values is learned.

What the layers do internally: each 3 × 3 convolution learns filters, padding 1 preserves 28 × 28, BatchNorm normalizes each channel and learns scale/shift parameters, and residual + x performs elementwise addition.

For most applied image projects, recreating AlexNet or training ResNet from random weights is not the first choice. A model pretrained on a large image collection has already learned useful visual features. Replace its classifier for your classes, begin with conservative fine-tuning, and validate latency, memory and accuracy on your own data.
Counting names instead of tensors
Trace N×C×H×W and the shortcut shape through every stage. A familiar block name does not prevent a dimension error.
Assuming deeper always means better
Optimization, data size, regularization, compute and task difficulty matter. Compare validated systems, not layer counts.
Using historical preprocessing blindly
Use the preprocessing specified for the exact pretrained weights. Input size and normalization differ across model families.
Comparing parameter count alone
Latency depends on operation type, resolution, hardware, memory movement and implementation—not just parameters.
Forgetting the classifier head
A 1,000-class ImageNet head does not match a four-class project. Replace and train the final layer deliberately.
Loading weights into the wrong variant
Match architecture, version and weight enum; strict loading errors often reveal a real mismatch rather than an inconvenience.

captions: Each model inherited ordinary convolutional building blocks. Its historical importance comes from a design or training choice that made a new scale of visual learning practical.

Channel counts such as 6 and 16 were selected by the model designers. Spatial sizes such as 28 and 10 are consequences of the filter and padding choices. The final 10 is dictated by the task because the possible labels are digits 0–9.
Real multi-channel parameter counts also depend on the number of input and output channels, so the simplified 25-versus-18 comparison is not a complete layer count.

Small and larger filters capture different spatial scales. The 1 × 1 convolutions before expensive branches reduce channel count, so multi-scale processing costs less than applying every large filter to every input channel.

The 1 × 1 layer multiplies and adds across all 192 channels at each position, learning 16 useful mixtures. The following 5 × 5 filters process those 16 mixtures instead of all 192 maps, reducing this simplified branch count by almost ten times.
The shortcut is usually an identity map when shapes match. If width, height or channel count changes, a learned projection such as a 1 × 1 convolution can align the shapes before addition.

import torch
from torch import nn

class BasicResidualBlock(nn.Module):
    def __init__(self, channels):
        super().__init__()
        self.main = nn.Sequential(
            nn.Conv2d(channels, channels, 3, padding=1, bias=False),
            nn.BatchNorm2d(channels),
            nn.ReLU(),
            nn.Conv2d(channels, channels, 3, padding=1, bias=False),
            nn.BatchNorm2d(channels),
        )
        self.relu = nn.ReLU()

    def forward(self, x):
        residual = self.main(x)   # learn F(x)
        return self.relu(residual + x)  # add identity path

block = BasicResidualBlock(channels=32)
x = torch.randn(8, 32, 28, 28)
y = block(x)
      print(y.shape)  # torch.Size([8, 32, 28, 28])

headings.text: Choose the Output Before Choosing the Model
A Detector Predicts What, Where and How Confident
Why One Object Can Produce Several Boxes
Segmentation Predicts a Class at Pixel Resolution
Grad-CAM Explains a Class Score With a Coarse Heatmap

paragraphs.text: Deep Learning · Visual Understanding

Classification tells us what an image contains. Many real systems must also say where each object is, which pixels belong to it, or which regions influenced a prediction. This lesson separates those questions, calculates bounding-box overlap, explains duplicate removal, follows an encoder–decoder segmentation network, and computes a small Grad-CAM heatmap without treating it as proof.

A warehouse camera may need to answer "is a helmet visible?" That is classification. If it must count workers without helmets, it needs a location for each person: object detection. If a robot must grasp the exact visible shape of every package, boxes are too coarse and instance masks are more useful.
Four questions produce four different outputs
The same street scene is represented differently according to the task.

A bounding box is commonly stored as its top-left and bottom-right coordinates: (x min , y min , x max , y max ). The origin is usually the top-left of the image; x grows right and y grows down. A detector returns many candidate boxes, each with class scores and a confidence/objectness value.
Class
What object might be here?
forklift
Box
Where is it?
Score
How strongly did the model support it?

The box numbers are model-produced pixel coordinates: left x=120, top y=45, right x=310 and bottom y=220. The score 0.87 is also produced by the model. A developer chooses a score threshold that decides whether this candidate is shown; the threshold is not learned automatically by this output.

Training usually combines several losses. A classification term teaches the class, a localization term teaches box coordinates, and some detectors add objectness or mask losses. Their weights affect the trade-off; a low total number is meaningful only with the exact loss definition and validation metrics.
Simplified multi-task loss
L total = L class + λ box L box + λ obj L objectness

Each λ is a developer-selected hyperparameter that controls a term's relative contribution. It is multiplied by a loss because the raw terms can have different scales and priorities. The exact losses, weights and matching process differ across detector families.
class loss 0.40
box loss 0.20 × λ=5
objectness 0.10 × λ=1

These small values and weights are manually chosen only to demonstrate the arithmetic. During real training, the model produces the three losses from its predictions and labels; the training configuration supplies the λ values.
A predicted box can name the right class but be badly placed. Intersection over Union (IoU) compares its overlap with a labelled ground-truth box while accounting for their combined area.
Intersection over Union measures box overlap
Intersection over Union
IoU = area(A ∩ B) / area(A ∪ B)
The union includes every point covered by either box, counting the overlap once.
IoU = 1 means identical boxes; 0 means no overlap. A threshold such as 0.5 is a task/evaluation choice, not a universal definition of a correct detection.
Ground truth A = (10, 10, 50, 50). Prediction B = (30, 20, 70, 60). Coordinates are (x min , y min , x max , y max ).
2. Intersection width=min(50,70)−max(10,30)=20 height=30 area=600
Interpretation: only about 23.1% of the combined covered region overlaps. At IoU threshold 0.5 this prediction would not match the ground-truth object.

Detectors examine many locations, scales or region proposals. Several candidates can surround the same car. Non-maximum suppression (NMS) is a post-processing step that keeps a high-scoring box and suppresses lower-scoring boxes of the same class that overlap it too strongly.
Non-maximum suppression turns duplicate proposals into cleaner detections
1 · Rank
2 · Keep A
highest confidence
3 · Compare
4 · Suppress B
keep A and C

One-stage detectors such as YOLO, SSD and RetinaNet predict dense boxes/classes in one main pass and are often chosen for speed. Two-stage detectors such as Faster R-CNN first generate promising regions, then classify/refine them; they can offer strong accuracy but often cost more latency. This is a family-level tendency, not a guarantee for every model and device.

A semantic segmentation model produces a C × H × W grid of logits: C class scores at every pixel location. C is chosen from the number of categories in the task; H and W are the output grid's height and width. During training, the target is an H × W grid of class IDs supplied by the labelled mask.
A U-Net preserves detail while learning context

In the teaching diagram, 128 → 64 → 32 is caused by two downsampling steps that each halve height and width. The channel counts 32 → 64 → 128 are designer-selected capacities, not spatial measurements. The decoder reverses the spatial changes, while skip connections copy same-resolution encoder features across so boundary detail is available again.

U-Net uses an encoder to build context and a decoder to restore resolution. Same-scale skip connections recover fine detail. DeepLab families use atrous (dilated) convolution and multi-scale context so filters see wider regions without downsampling as aggressively. Mask R-CNN extends a detector with a mask branch for each detected instance.
Pixel IoU for one class
IoU = TP / (TP + FP + FN)
TP: correctly predicted class pixels; FP: extra predicted pixels; FN: missed class pixels.
Dice coefficient
Dice = 2TP / (2TP + FP + FN)
Dice emphasizes overlap and ranges from 0 to 1 under this definition.

A classifier gives a label but no box. Grad-CAM uses gradients of one selected class score with respect to a convolutional feature tensor. It averages those gradients to assign one importance weight to each feature channel, combines the channel maps, and applies ReLU so positive support remains.
Grad-CAM asks which final feature-map regions supported one class score
product image
class logit
"defective"
gradients
weight feature maps
coarse heatmap
Grad-CAM for class c
α k c = (1/Z) Σ i,j ∂y c /∂A i,j k L c = ReLU(Σ k α k c A k )

A k is feature map k produced by the model, y c is the selected class logit, Z is the calculated number of spatial cells, and α is that map's average sensitivity for class c. Division by Z turns a sum over locations into an average so channel weights remain comparable across the map.

We manually choose the two small feature maps so every cell is visible. Backpropagation would calculate four class-score gradients per map; averaging those four gradients produces α₁=0.5 and α₂=−0.25 for this teaching example.
A₁=[[1,2],[0,1]], A₂=[[0,1],[2,1]] weight and add matching cells: 0.5A₁−0.25A₂ = [[0.50,0.75],[−0.50,0.25]] keep positive support with ReLU: Lᶜ=[[0.50,0.75],[0,0.25]]

Interpretation: the top-right cell provides the strongest positive support for class c in this coarse map. A negative combined cell becomes zero; Grad-CAM is showing supporting evidence, not a pixel-accurate object mask.

Detection evaluation must match predicted boxes to ground truth at an IoU threshold. Precision asks how many reported detections were correct; recall asks how many labelled objects were found. Varying the confidence threshold creates a precision–recall curve. Average Precision (AP) summarizes that curve for a class under a specified evaluation protocol; mAP averages AP across classes and sometimes across multiple IoU thresholds.
This PyTorch example loads both pretrained weights and their matching preprocessing. A detector expects a list of C × H × W image tensors and returns one dictionary per image.

For custom training, each target must contain correctly typed boxes of shape [N,4], integer labels, and optional [N,H,W] masks. In the pretrained torchvision detection convention, class index 0 represents background. Transform boxes and masks with the image.
Annotation cost
Boxes are slower to label than classes; high-quality masks are slower still. Ambiguous boundaries create disagreement.
Small and crowded objects
Downsampling removes detail, while NMS can suppress neighbouring instances. Report metrics by size and density.
Domain shift
Weather, camera, hospital or production-line changes can break performance even when benchmark mAP is strong.
Metric dependence
AP changes with IoU thresholds, class averaging, max detections and dataset protocol. State the exact metric.
Heatmap over-trust
Grad-CAM is coarse and class-specific. Use it for investigation with other tests, not as proof of model reasoning.
Real-time claims
Frames per second depends on resolution, batch size, preprocessing, post-processing, hardware and runtime. Measure end to end.

IoU measures geometric overlap and supports matching, NMS and evaluation.
NMS removes lower-scoring duplicate detections but needs careful thresholds in crowded scenes.
U-Net combines contextual encoding with detail-preserving skip connections.
Grad-CAM uses class gradients to weight feature maps and creates a coarse supporting-evidence map.
Choose the output and metric from the real decision the system must support.
captions: Semantic segmentation labels both cars as the same class. Instance segmentation additionally tells us that they are two distinct cars. Panoptic segmentation combines instance-aware "things" with semantic background "stuff."

With an NMS IoU threshold of 0.5, B is removed because it overlaps A heavily and has a lower score. C remains because it likely describes another object. Crowded objects can challenge greedy NMS; soft-NMS reduces scores instead of immediately deleting boxes.

The encoder sees larger context as resolution shrinks. The decoder upsamples. Skip connections concatenate corresponding encoder features so boundaries do not have to be reconstructed only from the smallest bottleneck.

A warm region means changing features there would strongly affect the selected class score. It does not prove causality, fairness or correct reasoning, and the final convolutional maps make the localization coarse.

from torchvision.models.detection import (
    fasterrcnn_resnet50_fpn_v2,

model.eval()

image = decode_image("warehouse.jpg")      # [C, H, W], uint8
input_image = weights.transforms()(image)   # matching preprocessing

with torch.no_grad():

labels = [weights.meta["categories"][i] for i in prediction["labels"]]
for label, score, box in zip(labels, prediction["scores"], prediction["boxes"]):
    print(label, round(float(score), 3), box.tolist())

headings.text: Vision Transformers: Reading an Image as a Sequence of Patches
Why Convert an Image Into Tokens?
Patch Size Controls the Sequence Length
The Class Token Collects Evidence for Classification
Self-Attention Lets One Patch Request Context From Others
One query attends to three patches
Multiple Heads and Encoder Blocks Build Richer Relationships
Smaller Patches Preserve Detail but Make Attention Expensive
CNN and ViT Encode Different Starting Assumptions
Use the Preprocessing Bundled With Pretrained Weights
When a ViT Is a Reasonable Starting Point
The ViT in One Connected Explanation

paragraphs.text: Deep Learning · Computer Vision

A Vision Transformer (ViT) replaces the CNN's sliding local filters with a Transformer encoder that relates image patches to one another. We will turn a picture into tokens, calculate the token count, explain class and position embeddings, perform one attention calculation, trace an encoder block, compare patch sizes, and use a pretrained ViT without claiming it always beats a CNN.

Imagine a satellite image containing a river, fields and a smoke plume. A CNN begins by applying small local filters; distant regions interact only after information crosses several layers. A Transformer offers another route: represent image regions as a sequence and let each region directly weigh information from every other region through self-attention .

A Transformer was originally designed for sequences, not a height-by-width pixel grid. Passing one token per pixel would make the sequence enormous. ViT therefore groups nearby pixels into fixed, non-overlapping patches . Each patch is flattened and mapped to a fixed-length embedding vector. The result looks like a sequence of visual tokens.
ViT turns a two-dimensional image into a sequence of patch tokens
This 3 × 3 teaching image becomes nine patch tokens. Real models commonly use many more.

For an H × W image and square P × P patches, the number of patch tokens is (H/P) × (W/P), assuming the dimensions divide evenly. The original ViT naming convention uses labels such as ViT-B/16: a Base-sized Transformer with 16 × 16 patches.
Number of patch tokens
N = (H × W) / P²
H and W are image height and width, P is patch side length, and N excludes any special class token.
1. Patches per side 224 / 16 = 14
2. Patch tokens 14 × 14 = 196
3. Sequence length 196 + 1 [CLS] = 197 tokens
values in one RGB patch = 16 × 16 × 3 = 768
A learned linear projection converts those 768 raw values into the model's embedding dimension D. D also happens to be 768 in ViT-Base, but that equality is a model choice, not a general rule.

ViT prepends one learned vector called [CLS] to the patch sequence. It contains no pixels. Across encoder layers, self-attention lets this token collect information from the patches. The final [CLS] representation is passed to a classifier that outputs image-level logits. Other architectures may pool patch tokens instead, so [CLS] is a design choice rather than a universal Transformer requirement.
Patch content alone does not say where it came from
Without position information, these two sequences contain the same token contents even though their layouts differ.
Ordered layout
Same content, shuffled

Each token is projected into three vectors. A query Q describes what this token is looking for. A key K describes what another token offers. Their dot product gives a compatibility score. A value V carries the information that will be mixed.
Where Q, K and V actually come from
Every patch first has a token vector X. The model owns three learned weight matrices. Multiplying X by each matrix creates three different views of the same token.
Token X
calculated from patch values, patch-projection weights and position
Query Q
X × W_Q
what this token is looking for
Key K
X × W_K
what each token can be matched on
Value V
X × W_V
the information each token can send
Scaled dot-product attention
Attention(Q,K,V) = softmax(QKᵀ / √d k )V
QKᵀ: multiply each query by every key and add matching vector components to measure compatibility.
÷ √d k : scale scores before softmax so wider vectors do not create unnecessarily extreme dot products.
softmax: exponentiate and divide by the row total to create positive weights that sum to 1.
× V: multiply each value vector by its weight and add them to create the requested context.

We manually choose two-number q, k and v vectors so the arithmetic remains visible. In a real forward pass, the learned projection matrices shown above calculate them. Here d k =2 because every query and key contains two numbers, so the scale is √2.

Interpretation: this query receives equal strong weight from patches 1 and 3, less from patch 2, then blends their value information. The two output numbers are the new context for this query in our tiny head.
An attention head creates a token-to-token weight table
Each row sums to 1. Darker cells receive more value information for that query token in this illustrative head.

Multi-head attention runs several learned query/key/value projections in parallel. One head might become sensitive to colour continuity while another relates distant object parts; these interpretations are not guaranteed labels. Head outputs are concatenated and projected. A token-wise MLP then transforms each representation, while LayerNorm and residual shortcuts stabilize deep stacks.
Embedding width D = 768 chosen by the ViT-Base design
Heads h = 12 also an architecture choice
d k = D/h = 64 calculated width per head
12 × 64 = 768 concatenation restores D
One Transformer encoder block updates every token
token sequence
patch + position
LayerNorm
stabilize values
Multi-head attention
tokens exchange context
Add shortcut
preserve input
LayerNorm + MLP
transform each token
block output

LayerNorm changes the distribution of values but keeps the token shape. Attention and the MLP also return width D so their outputs can be added to the residual path position by position. In ViT-Base, the MLP's hidden width 3,072 is a designer-selected expansion—four times 768—before a second learned layer returns it to 768.

After one block, every patch token contains its original visual information plus context gathered from other tokens. Repeating blocks refines those representations. For classification, the final normalized [CLS] token is sent through a linear head to produce class logits.

Standard global self-attention compares every token with every token, creating an N × N score matrix per head. Halving patch width gives four times as many 2D patches and roughly sixteen times as many token-pair scores.

The table omits [CLS], batch, head and embedding dimensions, but accurately shows the quadratic token relationship. Hierarchical/windowed designs such as Swin restrict attention regions to reduce cost for high-resolution vision.

"ViT sees globally" does not mean it automatically understands every long-range relationship, and "CNN is local" does not mean later CNN layers cannot represent global context. Architecture, scale, pretraining, augmentation and optimization all matter. For a modest dataset, comparing pretrained models is more useful than repeating universal claims.

A pretrained ViT expects the resolution, scaling and normalization used during its training. Torchvision weight objects provide matching transforms and class metadata, reducing silent preprocessing mismatch.
After the new head learns, optionally unfreeze later encoder blocks and fine-tune with a smaller learning rate. Freezing is not permanent: it is a staged starting strategy that should be validated.
Strong pretrained checkpoint exists
A ViT can transfer rich patch relationships even when your labelled dataset is modest.
Long-range image context matters
Global attention can connect separated regions directly, though task evidence must confirm the benefit.
High-resolution dense prediction
Prefer a hierarchical/windowed vision Transformer or hybrid; plain global attention may be too expensive.
Tiny edge deployment
Benchmark lightweight CNNs and compact/hybrid Transformers. Parameter count alone does not determine latency.
Learning the basics
Implement a tiny patch embed and attention block, but do not expect from-scratch toy training to match a pretrained system.
Need reliable explanation
Attention is not sufficient. Pair model choice with task-specific interpretability and validation methods.

captions: A patch token is not a label such as "wheel." It is a learned vector representation of raw patch values. The Transformer updates each vector by exchanging information with the other tokens.
ViT adds a learned position vector to every patch embedding. It can therefore distinguish "sky at the top" from the same sky-coloured patch placed near the road.

Different heads use different learned query, key and value projections, so they can model different relationships. Individual attention weights should not automatically be interpreted as faithful explanations of a model decision.

Attention mixes information across tokens. The MLP—two dense layers with a nonlinearity—processes each token position independently. Residual shortcuts make both sublayers learn changes to their inputs.
